title: Elodie and the Harvest
premise: August Kavanagh, a rationalist teacher at Hollowmere School where students keep vanishing from the rolls without explanation, inherits his grandmother's house and discovers every old family photograph now contains an empty chair that wasn't there before. The chair is a summons: the Kavanagh line was bound generations ago to 'the Count,' an entity that harvests one family member per generation, and his grandmother's death has left the papers unsigned. August must reconcile with the estranged cousins he disowned years ago — his found-and-lost family — and get them all beyond the town's boundary before the last resident of the house signs the inheritance papers, which would legally bind him as the next offering. In the end August burns the unsigned papers in the hearth his grandmother kept lit for sixty years, breaking the contract but not the entity's attention; the family escapes together, though August stays behind as the new keeper, trading himself for their freedom.
about_author: Edmund Almeida is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who spent nine years in small-town classrooms before turning to horror full-time. His work draws on the quiet dread of declining farming communities, where empty houses outnumber occupied ones and everyone remembers who left and who stayed.

chapters.title: The Missing Roster
chapters.summary: POV August. Arriving at Hollowmere School, August notices the attendance ledger lists eleven students but only eight desks are ever occupied, and no one will discuss the discrepancy. The principal hands him a folder of 'transfers' with blank destination lines. Emotional beat: unease masked by professional detachment — August decides it's bureaucratic sloppiness, nothing more.

chapters.title: Grandmother's House
chapters.summary: POV August. After news of his grandmother's death, August returns to the family farmhouse he fled fifteen years ago after a bitter falling-out over her 'superstitions.' The lawyer mentions unusual paperwork: a deed contingent on 'all residents accounted for.' A neighbor warns him the hearth must never go cold. Emotional beat: grief tangled with old resentment.

chapters.title: An Extra Chair
chapters.summary: POV August. Sorting photographs, August finds that every image — spanning decades — now includes a plain wooden chair against the far wall that appears in none of his memories. When he photographs the photos, the chair sits closer. That night, a student from his class is absent, then struck from the roster entirely. Emotional beat: the first crack in his disbelief.

chapters.title: The Cousins
chapters.summary: POV alternating August and cousin Maren. Maren arrives uninvited, having felt 'the pull' through her own dreams, dragging two reluctant siblings. Old wounds reopen — August once testified against the family's practices in a custody dispute. But Maren shows him the family ledger: names, dates, one harvested per generation, always after the papers sign. Emotional beat: hostility giving way to shared fear.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Counts
chapters.summary: POV Maren. Maren deciphers the ledger's arithmetic: the Count doesn't take randomly — it takes whoever is 'resident' when the inheritance finalizes, and residency is defined by blood, proximity, and acknowledgment. August's return plus the cousins' arrival has made them all countable. A second student disappears; the school quietly closes a classroom door. Emotional beat: dawning responsibility.

chapters.title: Boundary Lines
chapters.summary: POV August. The cousins test escape: crossing the county line, Maren's youngest brother begins to fade like a bad photograph until they turn back. The binding holds within the township. August researches the original contract in the church archive and finds his grandmother's signature — dated sixty years ago, witnessed by a name still on the school roster. Emotional beat: claustrophobia; the trap is legal, not supernatural alone.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: POV August. The lawyer arrives to finalize probate: if August signs, the house — and the obligation — passes formally to him, and the Count may collect immediately. August stalls, claiming missing documents. That night the chair appears in the room with him, close enough to touch, and something patient sits in it. Emotional beat: terror fused with temptation — signing would end the uncertainty.

chapters.title: Sixty Years of Fire
chapters.summary: POV Maren. Maren learns from the neighbor why the hearth never went out: the fire is the contract's anchor, and grandmother kept it burning to keep the collection date perpetually deferred. But the flame gutters now that she's dead. The cousins attempt to feed the fire with the ledger itself and it refuses to burn. Emotional beat: desperate ingenuity curdling into despair.

chapters.title: The Signing
chapters.summary: POV August. Climax. The Count forces the issue: the lawyer returns compulsion-driven, pen in hand, and the youngest cousin begins fading even indoors. August realizes the contract requires a willing Kavanagh signature — so he signs, but writes himself as sole heir, severing the others' residency. He orders them across the boundary; they hold there, solid, screaming at him to run too. Emotional beat: sacrifice as the ultimate act of loyalty and truth-telling.

chapters.title: Keeper of the Hearth
chapters.summary: POV August, epilogue letters from Maren. The family watches from beyond the line as August feeds the fire and settles into the chair — which is now simply a chair. He reopens the schoolhouse for the remaining children, teaching under a new arrangement he doesn't fully understand. Final image: a new photograph on the mantel shows the whole family, together, with one chair standing empty and warm. Emotional beat: sorrow braided with hard-won belonging.
